newsitem.title: CHINA: China seven-year bond opens below issue price.
newsitem.headline: China seven-year bond opens below issue price.

text.p: China's first seven-year treasury bond, making its debut on the Shanghai stock exchange on Thursday, opened at 99.90 yuan, to become the first T-bond this year to trade below its issue price of 100 yuan, traders said.
A few minutes after trading, the bond hit an intraday low of 98.53 yuan before recovering slightly in early trade.

Traders said the bond, bearing a much higher coupon than bank interest rates, had been hit by Beijing's demand for tighter liquidity with the approach of the year-end and a bull-run on China's stock markets.

The People's Bank of China, the central bank, has instructed state banks and financial institutions to ensure a tight hold is kept on money supply with the year-end drawing near, which has capped liquidity flowing into the T-bond spot market, they said.
"The bond is the first this year to trade below its issue price due to the instructions," said one trader. "But room for further falls will be limited due to its high returns."
The bond, the last batch of China's state debt issue this year, has a coupon of 8.56 percent, 1.09 percentage points higher than the annual rate of 7.47 percent for one-year bank deposits.
Interest on the new bond will be calculated as from November 1 and paid on an annual basis instead of at maturity, allowing buyers to re-invest their money during the life of the bond.
A total of 20 billion yuan worth of the seven-year T-bond were issued from November 1 to Wednesday, bringing total T-bill and T-bond issues in China this year to a record high of 220 billion yuan.
In the first few days of issue, the high return and the promise of liquidity made the bond attractive to individual investors.

But it became increasingly less attractive as the listing date drew near and underwriters want to sell it in order to raise money to meet monetary requirements set by the central bank before the end of the year, industry sources said.
Another bearish factor for the T-bond is the continuing bull-run on China's two domestic A share markets, which has sucked money out of the T-bond spot market, traders said.
Shanghai's A share index has risen more than 100 percent this year and its Shenzhen counterpart nearly 300 percent.
